About this citation

Epictetus wrote nothing. The Discourses were transcribed and edited by his pupil Arrian, who states that he recorded what he heard and left the reasoning as it stood; the Handbook is Arrian's own selection. Attribution to Epictetus is therefore via Arrian in every case.

### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“It is not things that disturb people, but their judgments about things.”

Ancient Greek / English tradition

“ταράσσει τοὺς ἀνθρώπους οὐ τὰ πράγματα, ἀλλὰ τὰ περὶ τῶν πραγμάτων δόγματα.”

Enchiridion 5. English often says “judgments” or “opinions” for δόγματα — both are defensible; “things” for πράγματα keeps the Stoic contrast between externals and assents.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “It is not things that disturb people, but their judgments about things.”
-   “Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them.”

### Attribution notes

Epictetus, Enchiridion 5 (via Arrian). The Elizabethan-sounding “Men are disturbed not by things…” is a common older English rendering of the same Greek; both point to the same section. Crediting Marcus Aurelius is a frequent mix-up driven by Meditations' popularity, not by the text.

#### About Epictetus

Epictetus (c. 50–c.

### Interpretation

This is the opening move of the Enchiridion and the premise of Stoic therapy. Epictetus separates the event from the judgement about it — "my son is dead" is one thing, "this is a disaster" is an addition. His claim is that disturbance is caused by the addition, not the event, and that the addition is something we supply. The point is not that loss is unreal but that our reaction contains a claim we have not examined.

#### Why it matters

The practical version is to state what happened without the verdict attached. That separation is where a response becomes a choice rather than a reflex.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “It is not things that disturb people, but…”?

“It is not things that disturb people, but…” comes from Discourses and Enchiridion, 5 (c. 108 CE (recorded by Arrian)), attributed to Epictetus.

#### What does Epictetus mean by desire?

Ethics and moral psychology analyze appetite, love, ambition, and addiction. Stoic, Buddhist, and psychoanalytic traditions treat desire as trainable rather than merely given. This passage enters that discussion through desire, freedom.

#### Is the wording of this Epictetus quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “It is not things that disturb people, but their judgments about things.” Forms in circulation that differ: It is not things that disturb people, but their judgments about things. / Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them. The Ancient Greek / English tradition reads “ταράσσει τοὺς ἀνθρώπους οὐ τὰ πράγματα, ἀλλὰ τὰ περὶ τῶν πραγμάτων δόγματα.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Epictetus, Enchiridion 5 (via Arrian). The Elizabethan-sounding “Men are disturbed not by things…” is a common older English rendering of the same Greek; both point to the same section. Crediting Marcus Aurelius is a frequent mix-up driven by Meditations' popularity, not by the text.
